options.content: The value of the next best alternative given up
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The total cost of all the inputs a farmer buys
options.rationale: That is total cost, not opportunity cost.

options.content: The price a farmer pays for land
options.rationale: That is the price of land.

options.content: The sum of every alternative the farmer could choose
options.rationale: Only the single best alternative counts.

explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.

stem: According to the law of demand, what happens to the quantity demanded when the price of a product rises (other things equal)?

options.content: It falls
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: It rises
options.rationale: This is the direction for supply.

options.content: It stays the same
options.rationale: Quantity demanded responds to price.

options.content: It doubles
options.rationale: No fixed amount is stated by the law.

stem: On a graph with price on the vertical axis, how does a normal **supply** curve slope?

options.content: Upwards from left to right
options.rationale: Correct: more is supplied at higher prices.

options.content: Downwards from left to right
options.rationale: This is the demand curve.

options.content: It is a flat horizontal line
options.rationale: That would mean any quantity at one price.

options.content: It is an upright vertical line
options.rationale: That would mean the same quantity at any price.

explanation: The law of supply: higher price, greater quantity supplied, so the curve slopes upwards.

stem: What is the **equilibrium price** in a market?

options.content: The highest price any buyer is willing to pay
options.rationale: This is not the market-clearing price.

options.content: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: The price fixed by adding a profit to the farmer's costs of production
options.rationale: Market price is set by supply and demand.

options.content: The lowest price at which any seller will sell
options.rationale: This is not the market-clearing price.

explanation: At equilibrium the market clears: there is no surplus or shortage.

stem: A severe drought greatly reduces the maize harvest, while demand for maize meal stays the same. What is likely to happen to the price of maize?

options.content: It falls, because demand falls
options.rationale: Demand has not changed.

options.content: It falls, because supply falls
options.rationale: Lower supply raises price.

options.content: It stays the same, as demand is unchanged
options.rationale: The change in supply moves the price.

options.content: It rises, because supply falls
options.rationale: Correct: a shortage pushes the price up.

explanation: Lower supply at an unchanged demand creates a shortage at the old price, so the price rises.

stem: Which change would most likely **increase the demand** for beef in a town?

options.content: A rise in the price of beef
options.rationale: This lowers quantity demanded.

options.content: A rise in the incomes of the town's people
options.rationale: Correct: richer buyers buy more meat.

options.content: A fall in the price of chicken
options.rationale: Chicken is a substitute, so beef demand falls.

options.content: Many cattle farmers selling their steers at the same time
options.rationale: This raises supply, not demand.

explanation: Income is a determinant of demand; a cheaper substitute (chicken) would reduce beef demand.
hints: Demand shifts when something other than beef's own price changes.

stem: A farmer in a dry area with low, unreliable rainfall grows sorghum and keeps goats instead of growing maize. Which group of factors mainly influenced this choice?

options.content: Social factors
options.rationale: Food preferences would favour maize, not sorghum.

options.content: Government factors
options.rationale: No policy is mentioned.

options.content: Transport factors
options.rationale: Transport is not the issue described.

options.content: Natural factors
options.rationale: Correct: rainfall limits what will grow.

explanation: Climate and soil (natural factors) limit the crops and livestock that can succeed.
hints: What is described about the area?

stem: A buyer fixes the price of a crop well **above** the equilibrium price. What is the most likely result?

options.content: A shortage, with buyers queuing for the crop
options.rationale: This happens when price is below equilibrium.

options.content: No change in the quantity supplied or demanded
options.rationale: Both respond to price.

options.content: Farmers producing less because the price is higher
options.rationale: Higher prices encourage more production.

options.content: A surplus of the crop that cannot be sold at that price
options.rationale: Correct: supply rises and demand falls.

explanation: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, leaving a surplus.
hints: Compare quantity supplied and demanded at the high price.

stem: Why does the market price of tomatoes usually change more sharply during the year than the price of maize grain?

options.content: Tomatoes are needed by far fewer people than maize is
options.rationale: This does not explain sharp changes.

options.content: Maize prices are always fixed by law
options.rationale: This is not generally true.

options.content: Tomatoes are perishable and cannot be stored long
options.rationale: Correct: sellers must sell quickly when supply is high.

options.content: Tomatoes take longer to grow than maize
options.rationale: Tomatoes are a shorter crop.

explanation: Grain can be stored and sold later, smoothing supply; perishable tomatoes flood the market at harvest, so prices swing.
hints: What can a grain farmer do that a tomato grower cannot?

stem: The opportunity cost of a choice is the total value of all the alternatives that were not chosen.
explanation: False. It is the value of the single next best alternative given up.

stem: Classify each factor that influences a farmer's choice of enterprise.
explanation: Natural (climate, soil), economic (capital, markets, prices), social (food habits, skills), government (policy, support).

stem: What is the name of the price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied?
At a price of US\$0.50 per kg, buyers want 8,400 kg of cabbages a week but sellers offer only 5,100 kg. Calculate the shortage, in kg.
explanation: Shortage = quantity demanded − quantity supplied = 8,400 − 5,100 = 3,300 kg. The price will tend to rise.
workedSolution: 1. Shortage = quantity demanded − quantity supplied = 8,400 − 5,100 = 3,300 kg. The price will tend to rise.

stem: A farmer can use his poultry house for broilers (expected gross margin US\$1,240 a year), layers (US\$980) or rearing vegetable seedlings (US\$1,110). He chooses layers. What is the opportunity cost of his choice, in US dollars?
explanation: The best alternative given up is broilers, worth US\$1,240. Adding both alternatives (US\$2,350) is wrong because he could only have chosen one of them.
workedSolution: 1. The best alternative given up is broilers, worth US\$1,240. Adding both alternatives (US\$2,350) is wrong because he could only have chosen one of them.
hints: Which is the best alternative he gave up?

stem: Explain why the quantity of a farm product demanded falls when its price rises.

points.description: At a higher price buyers can afford less with the same income.
Some buyers switch to cheaper substitutes (e.g. rice or potatoes for maize meal).
Some buyers stop buying altogether / buy only what they need most.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: When the price rises, buyers' money buys less, so they buy smaller amounts; some switch to cheaper substitutes, and some stop buying the product at all, so the total quantity demanded falls.

explanation: Income effect, substitutes, buyers leaving the market.
hints: Think about buyers' budgets and other products.

stem: Name **four** opportunities in the agriculture industry other than growing crops or keeping livestock.

points.description: Supplying inputs (seed, fertiliser, feed, chemicals, equipment).
Processing and value addition (milling, oil pressing, dairy products, abattoirs).
Marketing, transport, storage or export of produce.
Services: extension, veterinary work, research, teaching, finance and insurance, machinery hire, agro-tourism.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Selling seed and fertiliser; milling maize or pressing sunflower oil; transporting and marketing produce; working as an extension or veterinary officer.

explanation: Agriculture includes input supply, processing, marketing and services.

stem:
Tendai has one hectare of land, enough money for one crop and limited labour. His expected gross margins (assume these figures) are shown.

| Crop | Expected gross margin per ha (US\$) |
| --- | --- |
| Maize | 620 |
| Groundnuts | 840 |
| Sunflower | 510 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Tendai decides to grow maize. Calculate the opportunity cost of this decision, in US dollars.
parts.explanation: The best alternative given up is groundnuts: US\$840.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The best alternative given up is groundnuts: US\$840.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether Tendai is right to grow maize rather than groundnuts.

points.description: On money alone, groundnuts earn US\$220 more than maize, so maize has a high opportunity cost.
Maize is the family's staple, so growing it saves buying food (maize meal) at high prices.
Groundnuts need more labour (lifting, drying, shelling) and costly seed, which he may not have.
Groundnuts would add nitrogen to the soil and could be rotated with maize next season.
Market and risk: maize has a ready market and may be less risky locally; groundnut prices may vary.
Judgement: either choice can be justified; a reasoned conclusion weighing food security, labour and income (e.g. maize this year, groundnuts in rotation next year).

Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation or application.
